name: English I - Writing Focus
description: A foundational English course that builds core writing skills including paragraph structure, narrative and expository essays, grammar, vocabulary, and literary analysis, culminating in a reflective portfolio.

modules.title: Paragraph Writing
modules.objectives: Write a focused paragraph with a clear topic sentence, relevant supporting details, transitions, and a concluding sentence that reinforces the main idea. Students will analyze a model paragraph, identify the job of each sentence, and revise an unfocused draft into one coherent paragraph.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: On this module page, complete this self-check before the assignment. Model: “Morning practice builds confidence. I repeat difficult measures slowly. I mark mistakes in pencil. I play the passage again without stopping. By the end, the music feels manageable.” Identify its topic sentence and three supporting details. Then revise this unfocused paragraph so every detail supports one topic sentence: “Our school garden needs care. Tomatoes grow near the fence. My bus arrives at seven. Students water the beds. Fresh herbs improve lunch.”
modules.assignment: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about a memorable experience using a clear topic sentence, three supporting details, and a concluding sentence. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: drafts, annotations, quotations, analysis, or revised writing from the Paragraph Writing module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Narrative Essays
modules.objectives: Write a narrative essay with a clear beginning, middle, and end, using vivid details, pacing, dialogue, and reflection to communicate a central theme. Students will analyze how pacing and point of view shape a model narrative, then revise a scene so its details support a clear reflection.

modules.practiceNote: On this module page, complete this visible self-check before the assignment: outline one narrative scene, choose a consistent point of view, add one pacing change, and write one sentence explaining why the event matters.
modules.assignment: Write a 3-paragraph narrative essay about a challenge you faced and what you learned. Include at least one scene with sensory detail, one line of dialogue, and a final reflection explaining why the event mattered. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: drafts, annotations, quotations, analysis, or revised writing from the Narrative Essays module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Descriptive Writing
modules.objectives: Use sensory details and figurative language to create vivid descriptions of people, places, and events. Students will analyze how word choice creates a dominant impression, then revise a paragraph so its sensory details follow a deliberate spatial order.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.

modules.assignment: Write a 300-word descriptive essay about a place that matters to you. Submit: a spatial-order plan, an earlier paragraph draft, and the revised essay. Include: a one-sentence dominant impression, at least three location cues that make the spatial order visible, details from at least four senses, three examples of figurative language, and annotations that identify at least three revised details and explain why each one strengthens the dominant impression. Evaluation: the teacher will check spatial organization, sensory specificity, figurative language, consistency of the dominant impression, and visible improvement from draft to revision.

modules.title: Expository Essays
modules.objectives: Write clear, informative expository essays that explain a topic using facts, examples, and logical organization. Students will analyze the organization of a model explanation, then create a process essay whose transitions make the sequence and purpose clear.

Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. modules.title: Persuasive Writing
modules.objectives: Write a persuasive argument with a clear claim, relevant evidence, a fair counterargument, and a strong conclusion that explains why the reader should agree. Students will evaluate the relevance of evidence, explain how each detail supports the claim, and revise a rebuttal so it responds fairly to an opposing view.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.

modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL — Review argumentative essay structure and identify claims, evidence, and counterarguments.
modules.assignment: Write a persuasive essay on a school policy issue. Take a clear stance and support it with at least three pieces of evidence. Present the strongest reasonable counterargument fairly, answer it with a rebuttal tied to evidence, and end with a conclusion that explains why the reader should agree or act. Submit: the completed essay and one earlier draft or annotated revision. Include: a clear claim, three attributed pieces of evidence with reasoning, a fair counterargument, an evidence-based rebuttal, a strong conclusion, and a 100-word revision reflection naming one sentence, paragraph, or idea you improved. Evaluation: the teacher will check claim clarity, evidence relevance and attribution, reasoning, fair treatment of the opposing view, rebuttal strength, conclusion, and documented revision.

(14) She writes careful during revision. (15) If I would have checked the source, I would have noticed the error. (16) There is many reasons to revise. quizQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a topic sentence in a paragraph?
options: To state the main idea of the paragraph
quizQuestions.answer: To state the main idea of the paragraph
quizQuestions.explanation: A topic sentence introduces the main idea that the rest of the paragraph will support.

quizQuestions.question: Which part of a paragraph directly supports the topic sentence?
quizQuestions.answer: Supporting details
quizQuestions.explanation: Supporting details provide evidence or examples that develop the main idea.

quizQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a concluding sentence in a paragraph?
options: To introduce a new idea for the next paragraph
To restate the main idea and signal the paragraph's end
To list all the evidence used in the paragraph
To provide background context the reader needs
quizQuestions.answer: To restate the main idea and signal the paragraph's end
quizQuestions.explanation: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph by echoing the main idea stated in the topic sentence — students often confuse it with a transition (which links paragraphs) or a topic sentence (which opens a new idea).

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary purpose of a narrative essay?
options: To inform readers about a topic
To persuade readers to take action
To tell a story from the writer's perspective
quizQuestions.answer: To tell a story from the writer's perspective
quizQuestions.explanation: A narrative essay tells a personal story, often sharing an experience and insight gained.

quizQuestions.question: Which element is essential to a strong narrative essay?
quizQuestions.answer: A central conflict or challenge
quizQuestions.explanation: A compelling narrative includes a conflict or challenge that drives the story.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'point of view' refer to in narrative writing?
options: The perspective from which the story is told
quizQuestions.answer: The perspective from which the story is told
quizQuestions.explanation: Point of view determines who is telling the story and how events are perceived.

quizQuestions.question: What is the purpose of dialogue in a narrative essay?
options: To summarize the sequence of events for the reader
To reveal character personality and advance the story's action
To provide statistical support for the narrator's main claim
To replace sensory details with quoted speech
quizQuestions.answer: To reveal character personality and advance the story's action
quizQuestions.explanation: Dialogue shows how characters speak and interact, making them feel real and moving events forward. Students sometimes treat dialogue as decoration or think it serves the same purpose as a plot summary, but it is a distinct narrative technique that develops character voice.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main goal of descriptive writing?
options: To create a vivid picture in the reader's mind
quizQuestions.answer: To create a vivid picture in the reader's mind
quizQuestions.explanation: Descriptive writing uses sensory details and figurative language to paint a vivid image.

quizQuestions.question: Which literary device compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as'?
quizQuestions.answer: Simile
quizQuestions.explanation: A simile is a comparison using 'like' or 'as.' It points to the reading, grammar, or writing feature that makes the answer defensible.

quizQuestions.question: What are the five senses used in sensory details?
quizQuestions.answer: Sight, sound, smell, taste, touch
quizQuestions.explanation: Effective descriptive writing appeals to all five senses. This reinforces the Descriptive Writing idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Which term describes the emotional atmosphere created by descriptive writing?
quizQuestions.answer: Mood
quizQuestions.explanation: A correct response identifies "Mood" and connects it to the module context.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of an expository essay?
options: To inform and explain a topic clearly
quizQuestions.answer: To inform and explain a topic clearly
quizQuestions.explanation: Expository essays inform or explain a topic using facts and logical organization.

quizQuestions.question: Which is an example of an expository essay type?
quizQuestions.answer: Process (how-to) essay
quizQuestions.explanation: A process essay explains how to do something step by step, a classic expository form.

quizQuestions.question: What should the introduction of an expository essay include?
options: Background information and a thesis statement
quizQuestions.answer: Background information and a thesis statement
quizQuestions.explanation: The introduction provides context and ends with a thesis statement. Students need to recognize why Background information and a thesis statement matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'objectivity' mean in expository writing?
quizQuestions.answer: Presenting information without personal bias
quizQuestions.explanation: Objectivity means presenting facts neutrally without personal opinion. It points to the reading, grammar, or writing feature that makes the answer defensible.

quizQuestions.question: What is a claim in persuasive writing?
options: The writer's main argument or position
quizQuestions.answer: The writer's main argument or position
quizQuestions.explanation: A claim is the central argument the writer makes and defends throughout the essay.

quizQuestions.question: In Persuasive Writing, what is a counterargument?
options: An opposing viewpoint that the writer addresses
quizQuestions.answer: An opposing viewpoint that the writer addresses
quizQuestions.explanation: A counterargument presents the opposing side's position, which the writer then refutes.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of evidence best supports a persuasive claim through logic and data?
options: Pathos — emotional stories that connect with the reader's feelings
Ethos — personal anecdotes that show the writer's experience
Logos — facts, statistics, and structured reasoning
Syntax — sentence structure choices that emphasize key ideas
quizQuestions.answer: Logos — facts, statistics, and structured reasoning
quizQuestions.explanation: Logos targets the reader's reason, using verifiable data and logical argument to support a claim. Pathos targets feelings, ethos targets credibility, and syntax is a style device — confusing these appeal types is a common error in persuasive writing analysis.

quizQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a rebuttal in a persuasive essay?
options: To repeat the writer's claim in different words to reinforce it
To explain why the counterargument is less convincing than the writer's position
To introduce new evidence unrelated to the opposing viewpoint
To summarize the opposing view without addressing its weaknesses
quizQuestions.answer: To explain why the counterargument is less convincing than the writer's position
quizQuestions.explanation: A rebuttal responds to the opposing side by exposing its limitations or errors, which strengthens the writer's own claim. Simply restating your claim, ignoring the counterargument, or introducing unrelated evidence does not constitute a true rebuttal.

quizQuestions.question: What is the first step in the research process?
options: Choosing a topic and research question
quizQuestions.answer: Choosing a topic and research question
quizQuestions.explanation: Effective research begins with identifying a focused topic and a clear research question.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is considered a credible source?
quizQuestions.answer: A peer-reviewed academic journal
quizQuestions.explanation: Peer-reviewed journals are evaluated by experts before publication. It connects the correct answer to Research Basics and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'primary source' mean?
options: A source found first in a Google search
An original, firsthand source such as a diary or original research
quizQuestions.answer: An original, firsthand source such as a diary or original research
quizQuestions.explanation: Primary sources are original materials created at the time of study. It connects the correct answer to Research Basics and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: Why is it important to organize research notes by subtopic before drafting?
options: It allows the writer to copy sources directly without paraphrasing
It groups related information so drafting becomes more logical and efficient
It removes the need to read full sources rather than skimming
It satisfies a formatting requirement without affecting writing quality
quizQuestions.answer: It groups related information so drafting becomes more logical and efficient
quizQuestions.explanation: Organizing notes by subtopic clusters evidence and ideas around each body paragraph's focus, preventing disorganized drafts and reducing plagiarism risk. The other options describe shortcuts or misconceptions about the research process.

quizQuestions.question: In Citation & MLA, what does MLA stand for?
quizQuestions.answer: Modern Language Association
quizQuestions.explanation: MLA stands for Modern Language Association, which publishes style guidelines used in humanities courses.

quizQuestions.question: In MLA format, how are in-text citations typically formatted?
quizQuestions.answer: (Author Page)
quizQuestions.explanation: MLA in-text citations include the author's last name and the page number in parentheses.

quizQuestions.question: Which Works Cited entry is placed first when the authors are Chen, Garcia, and Patel?
options: Chen, because MLA alphabetizes by the first author's last name
Garcia, because the middle name is listed first
Patel, because the most recent source comes first
Whichever source appears first in the essay
quizQuestions.answer: Chen, because MLA alphabetizes by the first author's last name
quizQuestions.explanation: MLA Works Cited entries are alphabetized by the first meaningful element, usually the author's last name, so Chen comes before Garcia and Patel. Citation order in the essay and publication date do not control the list's order.

quizQuestions.question: Which revision is the best example of the “Move” step in ARMS?
options: Add a statistic to support the claim.
Place the explanation immediately after the evidence it analyzes.
Replace a vague verb with a precise verb.
quizQuestions.answer: Place the explanation immediately after the evidence it analyzes.
quizQuestions.explanation: In ARMS, Move changes the position of existing material to improve organization and clarity.

quizQuestions.question: What is the difference between revision and proofreading?
options: Revision focuses on content and organization; proofreading focuses on grammar and mechanics
quizQuestions.answer: Revision focuses on content and organization; proofreading focuses on grammar and mechanics
quizQuestions.explanation: Revision addresses big-picture issues; proofreading addresses surface-level errors. Students need to recognize why Revision focuses on content and organization; proofreading focuses on grammar and mechanics matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

quizQuestions.question: Why is peer review valuable in the revision process?
options: It allows the teacher to grade work
Fresh eyes can catch errors and unclear passages the writer may miss
quizQuestions.answer: Fresh eyes can catch errors and unclear passages the writer may miss
quizQuestions.explanation: Peer reviewers offer an outside perspective that identifies weaknesses the writer cannot see objectively.

quizQuestions.question: A student finds that her second paragraph begins with a weak, general sentence that buries the paragraph's best point in the middle. Which ARMS action addresses this problem?
options: Add — insert additional evidence after the weak opening sentence
Remove — delete the entire paragraph because the point is unclear
Move — reposition the strongest sentence to open the paragraph
Substitute — replace the paragraph with a completely new topic
quizQuestions.answer: Move — reposition the strongest sentence to open the paragraph
quizQuestions.explanation: The Move step addresses organizational problems by relocating content to a more effective position. Add inserts new material, Remove deletes weak content, and Substitute swaps an idea for a stronger one — each targets a different revision goal.

quizQuestions.question: What is a sentence fragment?
options: A sentence with too many words
An incomplete sentence that lacks a subject, verb, or complete thought
A sentence that is too formal
quizQuestions.answer: An incomplete sentence that lacks a subject, verb, or complete thought
quizQuestions.explanation: A sentence fragment is missing one or more essential components making it grammatically incomplete.

quizQuestions.question: What is subject-verb agreement?
options: Using the same verb tense throughout
Matching the subject and verb in number (singular/plural)
Placing the subject before the verb
quizQuestions.answer: Matching the subject and verb in number (singular/plural)
quizQuestions.explanation: Subject-verb agreement requires singular subjects use singular verbs and plural subjects use plural verbs.

quizQuestions.question: Which sentence demonstrates correct subject-verb agreement?
quizQuestions.answer: The dogs run fast.
quizQuestions.explanation: 'Dogs' is a plural subject and requires the plural verb 'run.' Students need to recognize why The dogs run fast. matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

quizQuestions.question: In Sentence Variety, what is a simple sentence?
options: A sentence with one independent clause
A sentence with two independent clauses
A sentence with a dependent clause
quizQuestions.answer: A sentence with one independent clause
quizQuestions.explanation: A simple sentence contains one independent clause expressing a complete thought.

quizQuestions.question: What is a compound sentence?
options: A sentence with one subject and multiple verbs
A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon
A sentence with a dependent clause
quizQuestions.answer: A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon
quizQuestions.explanation: A compound sentence combines two or more independent clauses using coordinating conjunctions or a semicolon.

quizQuestions.question: What makes a complex sentence different from a compound sentence?
options: A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least one dependent clause
A complex sentence uses more punctuation
A complex sentence has more subjects
quizQuestions.answer: A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least one dependent clause
quizQuestions.explanation: Complex sentences combine an independent clause with one or more dependent clauses.

quizQuestions.question: Why is sentence variety important in writing?
options: It creates rhythm and maintains reader interest
It avoids the need for punctuation
It is required by grammar rules
quizQuestions.answer: It creates rhythm and maintains reader interest
quizQuestions.explanation: Varying sentence structures creates rhythm and keeps readers engaged, preventing monotony.

quizQuestions.question: In Vocabulary Building, what is a context clue?
options: Information in the surrounding text that helps determine a word's meaning
quizQuestions.answer: Information in the surrounding text that helps determine a word's meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: Context clues are words or sentences near an unfamiliar word that provide hints about its meaning.

quizQuestions.question: In Vocabulary Building, what is a word root?
options: A base part of a word from which other words are formed
The last syllable of a word
quizQuestions.answer: A base part of a word from which other words are formed
quizQuestions.explanation: A word root is the core part of a word that carries its fundamental meaning.

quizQuestions.question: Which sentence uses an antonym context clue to help define the unfamiliar word 'garrulous'?
options: Maya was garrulous, chatting with strangers for hours.
Unlike her shy, reserved sister, Maya was garrulous and never stopped talking.
Garrulous, defined as 'excessively talkative,' appears in the glossary.
After two cups of coffee, Maya became garrulous.
quizQuestions.answer: Unlike her shy, reserved sister, Maya was garrulous and never stopped talking.
quizQuestions.explanation: The contrast signal 'unlike her shy, reserved sister' establishes an antonym clue — garrulous must mean the opposite of shy and reserved. The first sentence uses a restatement clue, the third is a direct definition clue, and the fourth provides no contrast or definition.

quizQuestions.question: In the word 'misinterpret,' which morpheme signals that a wrong action has occurred?
options: The prefix 'mis-' meaning wrongly or incorrectly
The root 'interpret' because it carries the core meaning
quizQuestions.answer: The prefix 'mis-' meaning wrongly or incorrectly
quizQuestions.explanation: The prefix mis- attaches to a root to signal an error or incorrect action (misinterpret = to interpret incorrectly). The root carries the action's core meaning, suffixes modify word endings, and vowel patterns do not signal negation — recognizing common prefixes helps decode hundreds of unfamiliar words.

quizQuestions.question: What is the 'main idea' of a passage?
options: The first sentence of the passage
The most important point the author is making
quizQuestions.answer: The most important point the author is making
quizQuestions.explanation: The main idea is the central message that all other details support. Students need to recognize why The most important point the author is making matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'making an inference' mean in reading?
options: Using clues from the text to draw a conclusion not directly stated
quizQuestions.answer: Using clues from the text to draw a conclusion not directly stated
quizQuestions.explanation: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from evidence in the text. It connects the correct answer to Reading Comprehension and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: What is the author's purpose in a text?
options: The reason the author wrote the text (to inform, persuade, or entertain)
quizQuestions.answer: The reason the author wrote the text (to inform, persuade, or entertain)
quizQuestions.explanation: Author's purpose refers to the writer's reason for creating a text. This reinforces the Reading Comprehension idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: After reading an article about urban noise, a student concludes: 'The author never says it directly, but this whole piece argues that city noise harms children's learning.' This student is applying which reading skill?
options: Summarizing — restating the article's key points in sequence
Identifying the main idea — locating the topic sentence
Making an inference — using text evidence to reach an unstated conclusion
Identifying author's purpose — deciding whether the text is fiction or nonfiction
quizQuestions.answer: Making an inference — using text evidence to reach an unstated conclusion
quizQuestions.explanation: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from textual evidence that the author never states outright. Summarizing restates what is stated; identifying a main idea finds an explicit central point; author's purpose addresses why a text was written, not what the reader independently concludes.

quizQuestions.question: What is a theme in literature?
options: The central message or insight about life conveyed by the work
quizQuestions.answer: The central message or insight about life conveyed by the work
quizQuestions.explanation: Theme is the underlying message or universal truth explored in a literary work.

quizQuestions.question: What is the 'plot' of a story?
options: The lesson learned from the story
The sequence of events that make up the story
The setting where the story takes place
The point of view of the narrator
quizQuestions.answer: The sequence of events that make up the story
quizQuestions.explanation: Plot refers to the series of events following exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.

quizQuestions.question: A character begins a story caring only about himself and ends it sacrificing everything for others. Which literary term best describes this type of character?
options: Static character — one who remains unchanged throughout the story
Flat character — one defined by only one or two simple traits
Dynamic character — one who undergoes significant internal change
Foil character — one who contrasts with another character to highlight their traits
quizQuestions.answer: Dynamic character — one who undergoes significant internal change
quizQuestions.explanation: A dynamic character experiences meaningful growth or change in values, attitude, or behavior over the course of a story. A static character stays the same; a flat character lacks complexity; a foil exists to contrast another character — distinguishing these terms is foundational to character analysis.

questions.question: What are the three essential parts of a paragraph?
options: Topic sentence, supporting details, concluding sentence
questions.answer: Topic sentence, supporting details, concluding sentence
questions.explanation: A well-structured paragraph consists of a topic sentence, supporting details, and a concluding sentence.

questions.question: Which essay type is primarily used to tell a personal story?
questions.answer: Narrative
questions.explanation: A narrative essay tells a personal story from the writer's own experience. The explanation models how students should justify a language-arts answer with textual or structural evidence.

questions.question: What is the purpose of sensory details in descriptive writing?
options: To create vivid images using the five senses
questions.answer: To create vivid images using the five senses
questions.explanation: Sensory details appeal to sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch to create a vivid experience.

questions.question: In an expository essay, what is the thesis statement?
options: A sentence that states the main point of the essay
The opening hook that grabs the reader's attention in the first sentence
A list of all the supporting details the body paragraphs will cover
The concluding sentence that restates the overall argument at the end
questions.answer: A sentence that states the main point of the essay
questions.explanation: A thesis statement signals the essay's central argument and typically appears at the end of the introduction. Students often confuse it with a hook (which opens the introduction), an outline of body points (which lists evidence), or a concluding sentence (which appears at the essay's end).

questions.question: Which appeal relies on emotion to persuade an audience?
questions.answer: Pathos
questions.explanation: Pathos is an emotional appeal that connects with the audience's feelings and sympathies.

questions.question: What does citing a source mean?
options: Giving credit to the original author by referencing their work
questions.answer: Giving credit to the original author by referencing their work
questions.explanation: Citing a source means acknowledging where you found information and giving credit to the original author.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between revision and editing?
options: Revision addresses content and organization; editing fixes grammar and mechanics
questions.answer: Revision addresses content and organization; editing fixes grammar and mechanics
questions.explanation: Revision focuses on improving ideas and structure; editing corrects surface errors.

questions.question: In standard American English, which sentence correctly treats the collective noun as one unit?
questions.answer: The team is winning.
questions.explanation: In standard American English, a collective noun such as team normally takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit: “The team is winning.” The question specifies American English because some other varieties allow plural agreement with collective nouns.

questions.question: What type of sentence contains one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses?
questions.answer: Complex
questions.explanation: A complex sentence combines one independent clause with at least one dependent clause.

questions.question: How do context clues help a reader understand an unfamiliar word?
options: A definition found in the glossary
Information near an unfamiliar word that hints at its meaning
A synonym listed in a thesaurus
questions.answer: Information near an unfamiliar word that hints at its meaning
questions.explanation: Context clues are surrounding words or sentences that help the reader infer meaning.

questions.question: What does MLA in-text citation typically include?
options: Author's last name and page number
questions.answer: Author's last name and page number
questions.explanation: MLA in-text citations are formatted as (LastName PageNumber). It connects the correct answer to English I - Writing Focus midterm concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement: The climax of a narrative is...
options: To state the main idea of the paragraph
The turning point or highest point of tension
questions.answer: The turning point or highest point of tension
questions.explanation: The best answer is The turning point or highest point of tension. It directly fits the prompt, while the other choices reflect different course ideas, incomplete definitions, or common mistakes.

questions.question: What does 'inference' mean in reading?
options: Drawing a conclusion from evidence in the text
questions.answer: Drawing a conclusion from evidence in the text
questions.explanation: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from text evidence combined with prior knowledge.

questions.question: In English I - Writing Focus midterm concepts, what is personification?
options: Giving human qualities to non-human things
questions.answer: Giving human qualities to non-human things
questions.explanation: Personification gives human characteristics to animals, objects, or ideas. This reinforces the English I - Writing Focus midterm concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: What is a 'credible source' in research?
options: A reliable, trustworthy source with verified information
A source that agrees with your argument
The longest article on the topic
questions.answer: A reliable, trustworthy source with verified information
questions.explanation: A credible source has been reviewed for accuracy and authored by an expert or reputable organization.

questions.question: Write a focused 6–8 sentence paragraph about a meaningful experience. Include a clear topic sentence, at least three relevant supporting details, transitions, and a concluding sentence. Then label each required part.
questions.answer: A complete response includes one focused topic sentence, at least three specific supporting details, logical transitions, and a concluding sentence that reinforces the main idea. Labels must correctly identify each part; equivalent well-structured responses are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Score the 1-point item as follows: 0.2 for a focused topic sentence, 0.2 for at least three relevant supporting details, 0.2 for logical transitions, 0.2 for a concluding sentence, and 0.2 for accurate labels. Accept equivalent well-structured responses; award each component independently.

questions.question: What is the theme of a literary work?
options: The central message or universal truth
questions.answer: The central message or universal truth
questions.explanation: Theme is the underlying message about life or human nature the author conveys.

questions.question: What does the ARMS revision strategy stand for?
questions.answer: Add, Remove, Move, Substitute
questions.explanation: ARMS is a revision framework: Add, Remove, Move, and Substitute. This reinforces the English I - Writing Focus final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: What is indirect characterization?
options: The author directly states a character's traits
The character's traits are revealed through actions, dialogue, and reactions
A summary of the character's history
A description of the character's appearance only
questions.answer: The character's traits are revealed through actions, dialogue, and reactions
questions.explanation: Indirect characterization shows personality through behavior, speech, and others' responses.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement: A hanging indent in MLA format is...
options: To state the main idea of the paragraph
The first line is flush left and subsequent lines are indented
questions.answer: The first line is flush left and subsequent lines are indented
questions.explanation: The best answer is The first line is flush left and subsequent lines are indented. It directly fits the prompt, while the other choices reflect different course ideas, incomplete definitions, or common mistakes.

questions.question: Which sentence structure contains two independent clauses and one dependent clause?
questions.answer: Compound-complex
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Compound-complex.

questions.question: What is the author's purpose?
options: The reason the author wrote the text
questions.answer: The reason the author wrote the text
questions.explanation: Author's purpose is the reason behind the writing—commonly to inform, persuade, or entertain.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a run-on sentence?
options: Two independent clauses joined without proper punctuation
A sentence with too many adjectives
A sentence that lacks a subject
questions.answer: Two independent clauses joined without proper punctuation
questions.explanation: A run-on sentence occurs when independent clauses are improperly connected.

questions.question: Which option best states the main idea of a text?
options: The most important point the author makes
To state the main idea of the paragraph
The first sentence of the passage
questions.answer: The most important point the author makes
questions.explanation: The best answer is The most important point the author makes. It directly fits the prompt, while the other choices reflect different course ideas, incomplete definitions, or common mistakes.

questions.question: What does 'ethos' mean in persuasive writing?
options: An appeal based on the writer's credibility
questions.answer: An appeal based on the writer's credibility
questions.explanation: Ethos establishes the writer's trustworthiness, expertise, or moral character. It connects the correct answer to English I - Writing Focus final concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary and secondary source?
options: Primary sources are online; secondary sources are printed
Primary sources are original materials; secondary sources analyze or interpret primary sources
questions.answer: Primary sources are original materials; secondary sources analyze or interpret primary sources
questions.explanation: Primary sources are firsthand evidence; secondary sources interpret or describe primary sources.

questions.question: Which revision provides the strongest evidence-based literary analysis?
options: The story is interesting and has many details.
The repeated locked door suggests the narrator feels trapped because it appears whenever she avoids a difficult choice.
The author uses words, sentences, and paragraphs.
The ending is good because it is the final part.
questions.answer: The repeated locked door suggests the narrator feels trapped because it appears whenever she avoids a difficult choice.
questions.explanation: The answer makes an interpretation and supports it with a specific recurring detail and its context, which matches the course’s introductory literary-analysis objective.

questions.question: What is the main effect of sentence variety on readers?
options: It creates rhythm and keeps readers engaged
It ensures that every sentence in a paragraph follows the same grammatical pattern
It is mainly useful in creative writing and unnecessary in academic essays
It is a technique for adding length to an essay without adding new ideas
questions.answer: It creates rhythm and keeps readers engaged
questions.explanation: Varying sentence structures creates a natural rhythm that maintains reader engagement and prevents prose from feeling monotonous. Using identical patterns makes writing feel mechanical; the other distractors reflect common misconceptions about the scope and purpose of sentence variety.

questions.question: In English I - Writing Focus final concepts, what is a simile?
options: Giving human traits to non-human things
questions.answer: A comparison using 'like' or 'as'
questions.explanation: A simile explicitly compares two unlike things using the words 'like' or 'as.'

questions.question: Revise this sentence for clarity and concision, then explain one change: “Due to the fact that the students were in need of more time, they made the decision to continue working for a longer period of time.”
questions.answer: Sample: “Because the students needed more time, they decided to keep working.” Accept equivalent concise revisions that preserve meaning. The explanation should identify a specific change, such as replacing wordy phrases or removing repetition.
questions.explanation: Score both the effective revision and the explanation of one concrete revision decision; multiple equivalent revisions are valid.

questions.question: Write a 120–150-word persuasive paragraph on a school issue. Include a clear claim, one relevant piece of evidence, a fair counterargument, and a rebuttal that explains why your claim still stands.
questions.answer: A complete response states a debatable claim, uses relevant evidence, represents an opposing view fairly, and answers it with logical reasoning. The paragraph must explain the connection between evidence and claim; wording and position may vary.
questions.explanation: Score the 1-point item in four equal 0.25-point parts: clear claim; relevant evidence with reasoning; fair counterargument; effective rebuttal. Accept any defensible position and wording that meet the four criteria.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement: The exposition in a story's plot is...
options: The background information introducing characters and setting
To state the main idea of the paragraph
questions.answer: The background information introducing characters and setting
questions.explanation: The best answer is The background information introducing characters and setting. It directly fits the prompt, while the other choices reflect different course ideas, incomplete definitions, or common mistakes.

questions.question: Source sentence by Maya Chen on page 42: “Regular revision helps writers discover what they actually mean.” Paraphrase the idea in your own words and integrate it with an MLA-style signal phrase and location citation.
questions.answer: Sample: Chen explains that writers often clarify their own thinking when they revise (42). Accept equivalent accurate paraphrases that name Chen in the signal phrase, include page 42, and do not copy the source sentence too closely.
questions.explanation: Score meaning accuracy, original wording, a signal phrase naming the author, and the page location. Equivalent paraphrases are acceptable.

questions.question: What is the function of a concluding sentence in a paragraph?
options: To restate the main idea and bring the paragraph to a close
questions.answer: To restate the main idea and bring the paragraph to a close
questions.explanation: A concluding sentence signals the end of the paragraph by summarizing or reinforcing the main idea.

questions.question: What distinguishes an expository essay from a persuasive essay?
options: Expository essays inform without taking a personal opinion; persuasive essays argue a position
questions.answer: Expository essays inform without taking a personal opinion; persuasive essays argue a position
questions.explanation: Expository essays present information objectively; persuasive essays advocate for a specific viewpoint.
